title: 5. Leading Operational KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk

epigraph.quote: The uncertainty exists in terms of how we can execute. So the business demand is not a concern.
epigraph.author: Dr. Tien Wu, Chief Operating Officer, ASE Technology Holding (Q2 2026 Earnings Call)

web_blocks.html: To track ASE without getting lost in quarterly noise, analysts should watch six leading operational KPIs. Together, they govern earnings power and capital risk. First is LEAP (Leading-Edge Advanced Packaging and Testing) revenue. It captures 2.5D/3D heterogeneous integration, FoCoS, CoWoS-related assembly, and high-end AI test [3]. LEAP scaled from ~$1.6 billion in FY2025 to a thrice-raised FY2026 target above $4.0 billion. Management lifted that target from $3.2B to $3.5B+, then $3.7B, and finally >$4.0B in October 2026 [3]. Management also projects another doubling in FY2027. Full-process CoWoS is scaling from $300M in 2026 toward >$1.0B in 2027, while Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) enters mass production in Q4 2026 (> $0.5B target in 2027) [3].

Second is ATM Gross Margin, which historically peaked near 24%–25% in legacy cycles (23.5% in FY2025) [5]. Crossing 30.6% in Q3 2026—a full quarter ahead of plan, with Q4 2026 guided another 100–200 bps higher—confirms LEAP's superior pricing and value-add economics [1][3]. Third is ATM Computing Mix. It climbed from ~22% of ATM revenue in early 2025 to 34% in Q3 2026, cutting reliance on mature smartphones (down from 48% to 38%) [2]. Fourth is Capital Expenditure Intensity (CapEx / Revenue and CapEx / CFO). Cash PP&E outlays jumped from NT$79.5 billion in FY2024 to NT$162.1–164.6 billion in FY2025. They surged to NT$249.8 billion in 9M 2026 alone (187% of 9M CFO), backing management's $11.5 billion FY2026 CapEx plan across 13 new fab builds and 8 expansions (~$4B facilities plus $6.5B–$7.5B equipment per TrendForce/Q3 disclosures) [1][3][4][6]. Fifth is EMS (USI) Operating Margin & Mix. Contrary to earlier assumptions of an automotive-led pivot, Q3 2026 Form 6-K filings show Consumer electronics remains USI's largest slice at 41% (up from 33% in Q1 2025) [1][2]. AI/cloud Computing doubled from 10% to 21%, Communication fell from 33% to 19%, Industrial stood at 12%, and Automotive eased from 10% to 6% [1][2]. EMS gross margin compressed to 8.3% in Q3 2026 (9.1% in FY2025), with Q4 2026 EMS revenue guided flattish QoQ and operating margin ~2% [1][2]. Sixth is Customer & Substrate Concentration. Audited FY2025 Form 20-F disclosures (Note 36c & Item 4) reveal far tighter concentration than headline summaries suggest [4]. ASE's single largest customer (Apple across ATM SiP and USI EMS) accounted for 25.0% of consolidated revenue (NT$161,282 million) in FY2025, down from 29.3% in FY2024 and 29.4% in FY2023 [4]. The top five customers represented 46.5% of revenue (48.4% in FY2024), and the top ten held 50% of trade receivables [4]. Meanwhile, internal operations supplied just 8.7% of IC substrates, leaving 91.3% reliant on external vendors [4].

web_blocks.takeaway: ATM LEAP and gross margin KPIs continue to outperform—confirmed by October 2026 ATM sales jumping 57.7% YoY—while $11.5B CapEx burn, 25% single-customer concentration, and thin ~2% Q4 EMS margin guidance require strict discipline.

web_blocks.html: Auditing management's execution from 2023 through November 2026 shows a consistent pattern: leadership issues conservative quarterly guidance, beats on ATM delivery, and raises CapEx aggressively [1][3][6]. In July 2026 (Q2 call), CFO Joseph Tung guided Q3 2026 consolidated revenue up 21%–22% sequentially, consolidated gross margin to 20.5%–21.5%, and ATM gross margin to 28%–29% [6]. Actual Q3 2026 results beat every line: consolidated revenue surged 27.8% sequentially to NT$244,161 million, consolidated gross margin hit 22.1%, operating margin reached 13.6%, and ATM gross margin broke 30.6% [1][2]. Management then guided Q4 2026 consolidated revenue up 6%–8% sequentially (ATM +11%–13% QoQ, ATM GM +100–200 bps, EMS flattish at ~2% operating margin), consolidated gross margin to 23%–24%, and operating margin to 14.5%–15.5% [1][2]. Post-cutoff monthly revenue data filed on November 10, 2026 (Form 6-K) confirms early Q4 tracking [27]. October 2026 consolidated net revenue reached NT$88,615 million (+0.6% MoM, +47.1% YoY; US$2,779 million, +40.4% YoY) [27]. ATM net revenue surged 7.9% sequentially and 57.7% YoY to NT$56,840 million (US$1,783 million, +50.5% YoY), even as implied EMS sales eased 10.4% MoM to NT$31,775 million [27].

web_blocks.title: CEO/COO & CFO Guidance vs. Delivery Audit (2025–2026)
paragraphs: FY2026 LEAP Target Progression: Guided initially to double from $1.6B (2025) to $3.2B (2026) → raised to $3.5B+ mid-year → raised to $3.7B → raised again on Oct 29, 2026 to >$4.0B as tool installations beat schedule [3]. As CFO Joseph Tung stated on the Q3 2026 earnings call: "Yes. As I said, we are upping our 2026 LEAP revenue from originally USD 3.7 billion that we mentioned last quarter to over USD 4 billion for this year." [3]
Q2 2026 Guidance for Q3 2026 vs. Actuals: Guided +21–22% QoQ consolidated revenue (Actual: +27.8%); Guided 20.5–21.5% consolidated GM (Actual: 22.1%); Guided 28–29% ATM GM (Actual: 30.6%) [1][6].

CapEx Discipline Watch: Management raised FY2026 CapEx from $10.5B (Q2 2026) to $11.5B (Q3 2026) [3][6]. On the Q3 2026 call, CFO Joseph Tung added: "For this year's CapEx, we are increasing our CapEx for the year from USD 10.5 billion to USD 11.5 billion now... At this point, I believe the CapEx spending for next year will be even larger than this year... Funding-wise, we will continue to use... multiple cost-effective sources for us to raise funds to support our growth." [3] Demand delivery is clear, echoing Dr. Tien Wu's Q2 remark ("With AI, the hardware requirement is new, insatiable...") [6], yet rising 2027 spending raises the multi-year ROIC hurdle.

book_paragraphs: If you want to track ASE Technology Holding like an insider rather than reacting to headlines, you only need to watch six operational dials on the dashboard. Think of them as the vital signs of the factory floor. First is LEAP revenue—the dollar volume flowing through ASE's Leading-Edge Advanced Packaging lines. In 2025, LEAP brought in about 1.6 billion dollars. Entering 2026, management predicted it would double to 3.2 billion. Then they raised it to 3.5 billion, then 3.7 billion, and on October 29, 2026, they lifted the full-year target past four billion dollars—with plans to roughly double it again in 2027. That is not hype; that is physical cleanroom output clearing bottlenecks.

The second dial is ATM gross margin. For decades, investors assumed twenty-four or twenty-five percent was the natural speed limit for outsourced chip packaging. In 2025, ATM gross margin was 23.5 percent. In Q3 2026, it hit 30.6 percent, a full quarter ahead of management's own schedule. Why? Because when you are one of the only qualified providers on earth for 2.5D AI packaging and Co-Packaged Optics, you stop pricing on cost-plus and start pricing on scarcity and engineering yield.

The third dial is the mix shift inside ATM. In early 2025, nearly half of ATM's revenue came from communications—mostly smartphones—while computing was just twenty-two percent. By Q3 2026, computing had surged to thirty-four percent, while communications moderated to thirty-eight percent. Meanwhile, over on the EMS side at USI—our fourth dial—we have to correct a widespread misreading of the segment charts: Consumer electronics remains USI's largest end-market at forty-one percent in Q3 2026, while AI and cloud Computing more than doubled from ten percent in early 2025 to twenty-one percent, Communication dropped from thirty-three to nineteen percent, Industrial held at twelve percent, and Automotive eased to six percent. The fifth dial is customer and supplier concentration, which the audited FY2025 Form 20-F quantifies starkly: ASE's single largest customer—widely recognized as Apple across SiP and EMS—generated NT$161.3 billion, or twenty-five percent of total company revenue in 2025, down from 29.3 percent in 2024; the top five customers together represent 46.5 percent of sales, and ASE relies on external vendors for 91.3 percent of its IC substrates.

That leaves the sixth dial—and it is the one that flashes amber even during a boom: capital expenditure intensity. In 2025, ASE spent NT$162.1 billion on property and equipment, consuming more than one hundred percent of its operating cash flow. In July 2026, CFO Joseph Tung pegged full-year 2026 capex at 10.5 billion dollars; three months later, on the October 29 Q3 2026 call, management raised it again to 11.5 billion dollars and signaled that 2027 spending will be larger still. As Joseph Tung told analysts verbatim on the Q3 call: 'We are upping our 2026 LEAP revenue from originally USD 3.7 billion that we mentioned last quarter to over USD 4 billion for this year... For this year's CapEx, we are increasing our CapEx for the year from USD 10.5 billion to USD 11.5 billion now. At this point, I believe the CapEx spending for next year will be even larger than this year... Funding-wise, we will continue to use multiple cost-effective sources for us to raise funds to support our growth.' That echoes COO Dr. Tien Wu's earlier Q2 warning that AI hardware demand creates a tight automation bottleneck—meaning capital discipline, not customer demand, is the test.

When you audit management's walk-the-talk record, they deserve high marks for ATM execution. In July 2026, CFO Joseph Tung guided Q3 revenue up twenty-one to twenty-two percent sequentially and ATM gross margin to twenty-eight to twenty-nine percent; three months later, ASE delivered nearly twenty-eight percent revenue growth and a 30.6 percent ATM gross margin—beating every single line of its own guidance. And the November 10, 2026 monthly revenue filing confirmed Q4 momentum started right on schedule: October consolidated revenue hit NT$88.6 billion, up 47.1 percent year-over-year, as ATM revenue leaped 7.9 percent month-over-month to NT$56.8 billion even while EMS cooled sequentially ahead of its guided two-percent operating-margin quarter. Your only job as a disciplined analyst is to keep one eye glued to that 11.5 billion dollar capex bill and twenty-five percent single-customer exposure, ensuring the machines being bolted to the floor in 2026 stay loaded in 2028.

Let us pause and ask what could trip up those six operational dials over the next twenty-four months. Two scenarios deserve your attention. First, watch the gap between LEAP tool installations and actual wafer arrivals: if hyperscalers digest AI server inventories or TSMC accelerates its own CoWoS-L expansion faster than expected, ASE's newly installed 2026 capacity could face temporary under-utilization, pulling ATM gross margins back from thirty percent toward the mid-twenties. Second, watch the USI EMS segment's automotive and industrial mix: while forty-one percent automotive exposure provides welcome stability today, global electric-vehicle production schedules can pause abruptly, which would expose USI's thin 2.9 percent operating margin. Tracking those six KPIs quarterly—rather than relying on narrative hype—will give you an early warning long before any slowdown hits the bottom line.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Management's operational execution in 2025–2026 has been exemplary: they beat Q3 2026 guidance across every metric and raised LEAP targets four times in a single year. Yet a 30.6% ATM gross margin paired with an $11.5B capex budget means ASE is sprinting up a steep capital staircase—one where demand visibility, not quarterly margin, is the ultimate risk.
